title: Boosting II — Gradient Boosting

blocks.t: From the notes
The algorithm, exactly as written
Gradient Boosting
1. The first prediction is simply the mean of the target column.
2. res1 = Actual - pred
3. For every new model we take the recent residual as target.

4. $\text{Prediction} = m_1 + \lambda m_2 + \lambda m_3 + \dots$
\quad where $\lambda$ = learning rate, normally 0.1.

The notes lay this out as a table you fill in column by column. Let us
fill it in with real numbers so nothing is abstract.

Read the columns in order. pred1 is a constant — the mean, $10$.
res1 = Actual - pred, so the first row's residual is $4-10=-6$. A small tree
is now fitted with res1 as its target, and its output is added
(shrunk by $\lambda$) to give pred2. The new residual res2 is smaller
in magnitude than res1 on every row. That shrinking is the whole algorithm.
The classification variant, as written

For classification, the model one prediction is
$\log\!\left(\dfrac{\text{odd counts}}{\text{even counts}}\right)$,
and we try to reduce the log error.

"Odd counts / even counts" is the notes' shorthand for
number of 1s divided by number of 0s — the odds. So the
constant we start from is the log-odds of the training set, and the loss we
descend is log loss instead of squared error. Everything else — fit to the
pseudo-residual, shrink by $\lambda$, add — is unchanged.
Why the residual is the gradient

We want an additive model $F_M(x)=\sum_{m=0}^{M}\lambda\, h_m(x)$ minimising
$\sum_i L\big(y_i,F(x_i)\big)$. We cannot differentiate with respect to a
function, so we do gradient descent in prediction space: at stage
$m$ the current predictions are $F_{m-1}(x_i)$, and the direction of steepest
descent for observation $i$ is
g_i = -\left[\frac{\partial L(y_i,F)}{\partial F}\right]_{F=F_{m-1}(x_i)} .
For squared loss $L=\tfrac12 (y-F)^2$,

\frac{\partial L}{\partial F} = -(y-F)
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
g_i = y_i - F_{m-1}(x_i) = \text{residual}_i .

So "fit the next tree to the residuals" is "take a gradient step".
The tree $h_m$ is a regressor trained on $(x_i,g_i)$; it is our best piecewise
constant approximation to the gradient field. We then move a fraction $\lambda$
of the way:
F_m(x) = F_{m-1}(x) + \lambda h_m(x).

This is why the algorithm is called gradient boosting rather than
residual boosting: the residual is only the gradient of one particular
loss. Change the loss and the "residual" changes with it — for absolute
error the pseudo-residual becomes $\operatorname{sign}(y-F)$, for log loss it
becomes $y_i - p_i$. The code and the tree fitting never change.

blocks.cap:
Top row: the running prediction $F_m$. Bottom row: the residuals it
leaves behind, with the tree that will be fitted to them drawn in purple. The
first model really is a flat line at the mean, and the residual MSE falls at
every stage.

Left: for squared loss the negative gradient is a straight line through
the residual — they are the same quantity up to a factor of 2. Middle:
measured effect of $\lambda$. Right: train and test $R^2$ diverge, so the number
of trees is itself a regularisation parameter.

blocks.t: The learning rate, measured

$\lambda$ buys accuracy with time. A small $\lambda$ means each tree
is only partly trusted, so no single tree can drag the model off course, and
many small corrections average out into a smoother fit. The cost is that you
need more of them. The middle panel above shows it exactly: $\lambda=1.0$ shoots
up fast and then degrades; $\lambda=0.03$ climbs slowly but ends up
highest. The notes' default of $0.1$ sits in the sweet spot.

There is a rough conservation law: halving $\lambda$ roughly doubles
the number of trees needed for the same fit. So $\lambda$ and n_estimators
must always be tuned together — tuning one with the other fixed will
mislead you.

"More trees is always better" is true for a random forest and
false for gradient boosting. A forest averages independent estimators, so
extra members only reduce variance. Boosting keeps reducing training error
until it fits the noise. The right panel above shows train $R^2$ still climbing
while test $R^2$ has already turned over. Always use a validation set with
early stopping (n_iter_no_change in sklearn).
Classification through log-odds

blocks.cap:
The notes' starting value for classification and how it behaves. A
balanced dataset starts at $\log 1 = 0$; a skewed one starts already leaning
towards the majority class.

blocks.t:
Work in log-odds space, $F(x)=\log\frac{p(x)}{1-p(x)}$, so that
$p=\sigma(F)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-F}}$. Log loss for one observation is
L = -\big[y\log p + (1-y)\log(1-p)\big].
Differentiating with respect to $F$ (not $p$) and using $\frac{dp}{dF}=p(1-p)$:

\frac{\partial L}{\partial F}
= \left(-\frac{y}{p}+\frac{1-y}{1-p}\right)p(1-p) = p - y .

So the pseudo-residual is $-\partial L/\partial F = y_i - p_i$: the label minus
the predicted probability. The initial constant is the $F$ that minimises total
loss, which is exactly
the notes' $\log(\text{odd counts}/\text{even counts})$.

One extra step exists in classification that regression does not need. The tree
is fitted in residual space but must output a value in log-odds
space, so each leaf value is replaced by
$\gamma_j = \frac{\sum_{i\in j}(y_i-p_i)}{\sum_{i\in j} p_i(1-p_i)}$, a single
Newton step. Libraries do this for you; it is why boosted classification is
sometimes called Newton boosting.
Code — built from scratch, then with sklearn

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor
from sklearn.datasets import make_regression, make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingRegressor, GradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score, log_loss

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. THE NOTES' TABLE, REPRODUCED EXACTLY
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "iq":      [ 90, 100, 110, 120, 130],
    "cgpa":    [8.0, 7.0, 9.0, 9.5, 9.8],
    "package": [  4,   6,  12,  15,  13],
})
X = df[["iq", "cgpa"]].values
y = df["package"].values.astype(float)

# STEP 1 -- "the first prediction is the mean of the target column"
pred = np.full_like(y, y.mean())          # -> 10.0 everywhere
print("pred1:", pred)

lam   = 0.1                                # "lambda = learning rate, normally 0.1"
trees = []

for stage in range(1, 4):
    # STEP 2 -- "res1 = Actual - pred"
    res = y - pred
    print(f"res{stage}:", np.round(res, 3))

    # STEP 3 -- "for every new model we take the recent residual as target"
    t = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=1).fit(X, res)   # a stump
    trees.append(t)

    # STEP 4 -- "Prediction = m1 + lambda*m2 + lambda*m3 ..."
    pred = pred + lam * t.predict(X)

print("final :", np.round(pred, 3), " actual:", y)

# Prediction on a NEW row uses the same accumulation:
def predict(Xnew, base, trees, lam):
    out = np.full(len(Xnew), base)
    for t in trees:
        out += lam * t.predict(Xnew)
    return out

print(predict(np.array([[115, 9.2]]), y.mean(), trees, lam))

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. GRADIENT BOOSTING FROM SCRATCH -- REGRESSION
#    (identical to the loop above, just wrapped up properly)
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
class MyGBRegressor:
    def __init__(self, n_estimators=100, learning_rate=0.1, max_depth=3):
        self.M, self.lr, self.depth = n_estimators, learning_rate, max_depth

    def fit(self, X, y):
        self.F0 = y.mean()                 # the constant first model
        F = np.full(len(y), self.F0)
        self.trees = []
        for _ in range(self.M):
            g = y - F                      # negative gradient of 0.5*(y-F)^2
            t = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=self.depth).fit(X, g)
            F += self.lr * t.predict(X)    # take a shrunken step
            self.trees.append(t)
        return self

    def predict(self, X):
        F = np.full(len(X), self.F0)
        for t in self.trees:
            F += self.lr * t.predict(X)
        return F

Xr, yr = make_regression(n_samples=800, n_features=10, noise=12, random_state=0)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(Xr, yr, test_size=0.3, random_state=0)

mine = MyGBRegressor(200, 0.1, 3).fit(Xtr, ytr)
lib  = GradientBoostingRegressor(n_estimators=200, learning_rate=0.1,
                                 max_depth=3, random_state=0).fit(Xtr, ytr)
print("scratch R2:", round(r2_score(yte, mine.predict(Xte)), 4))
print("sklearn R2:", round(r2_score(yte, lib.predict(Xte)),  4))   # near-identical

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. GRADIENT BOOSTING FROM SCRATCH -- CLASSIFICATION
#    "the model one prediction is log(odd counts / even counts)"
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
def sigmoid(z):
    return 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-z))

class MyGBClassifier:
    def __init__(self, n_estimators=100, learning_rate=0.1, max_depth=3):
        self.M, self.lr, self.depth = n_estimators, learning_rate, max_depth

    def fit(self, X, y):
        ones, zeros = (y == 1).sum(), (y == 0).sum()
        self.F0 = np.log(ones / zeros)        # log(odd counts / even counts)
        F = np.full(len(y), self.F0, dtype=float)
        self.trees = []
        for _ in range(self.M):
            p = sigmoid(F)
            g = y - p                          # pseudo-residual of LOG loss
            t = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=self.depth).fit(X, g)

            # Newton step: rescale each leaf into log-odds space
            leaf = t.apply(X)
            for node in np.unique(leaf):
                m   = leaf == node
                den = np.sum(p[m] * (1 - p[m]))
                t.tree_.value[node, 0, 0] = g[m].sum() / (den + 1e-9)

            F += self.lr * t.predict(X)
            self.trees.append(t)
        return self

    def decision_function(self, X):
        F = np.full(len(X), self.F0, dtype=float)
        for t in self.trees:
            F += self.lr * t.predict(X)
        return F

    def predict_proba(self, X):
        p = sigmoid(self.decision_function(X))
        return np.column_stack([1 - p, p])

    def predict(self, X):
        return (self.predict_proba(X)[:, 1] >= 0.5).astype(int)

Xc, yc = make_classification(n_samples=1200, n_features=12, n_informative=6,
                             weights=[0.7, 0.3], random_state=0)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(Xc, yc, test_size=0.3, random_state=0)

gc_mine = MyGBClassifier(150, 0.1, 3).fit(Xtr, ytr)
gc_lib  = GradientBoostingClassifier(n_estimators=150, learning_rate=0.1,
                                     max_depth=3, random_state=0).fit(Xtr, ytr)
print("F0 (log-odds):", round(gc_mine.F0, 4))
print("scratch logloss:", round(log_loss(yte, gc_mine.predict_proba(Xte)), 4))
print("sklearn logloss:", round(log_loss(yte, gc_lib.predict_proba(Xte)),  4))

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. EARLY STOPPING -- the correct way to pick n_estimators
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
gb = GradientBoostingRegressor(
        n_estimators=2000,
        learning_rate=0.05,
        max_depth=3,
        subsample=0.8,          # stochastic GB: rows sampled per tree
        validation_fraction=0.15,
        n_iter_no_change=25,    # stop after 25 rounds with no improvement
        tol=1e-4,
        random_state=0)
gb.fit(Xr, yr)
print("stopped after", gb.n_estimators_, "of 2000 trees")

# staged_predict lets you watch the curve yourself
scores = [r2_score(yte, p) for p in lib.staged_predict(Xte)]
print("best tree count:", int(np.argmax(scores)) + 1)
The knobs that matter

head: Parameter
Typical
What it actually controls
rows:
How much of each tree is trusted.
Lower = better, slower. Tune with n_estimators.

Number of gradient steps. Not
"more is better" — set by early stopping.

Interaction order. Depth 1 = additive model,
depth 3 = 3-way interactions. Boosting wants weak learners.

Rows per tree. $<1$ gives stochastic gradient
boosting: adds randomness, reduces variance and time.

Guards leaves from fitting a single noisy
point — important because leaves hold gradients, not labels.

blocks.t:
Deep trees in boosting. A random forest wants fully grown trees; a
booster wants stumps or near-stumps. If max_depth is large each tree
already fits most of the signal, the residuals collapse to noise after two or
three rounds, and the ensemble overfits immediately. If your boosted model is
worse than a forest, depth is the first thing to check.

Scaling. Gradient boosting is tree based, so it needs no
feature scaling — splits are thresholds, invariant to monotone transforms.
Standardising does no harm but wastes a pipeline step. It does not handle
raw NaN in sklearn's classic GradientBoosting* (the
HistGradientBoosting* variants do).
Everything on one page
Summary
The four lines from the notes are the whole algorithm.

items:
$r_i = y_i - F_{m-1}(x_i)$ — the residual, which is the negative
gradient of squared loss. For log loss it becomes $y_i-p_i$.
Fit a shallow tree $h_m$ with $r$ as its target.

blocks.t:
Bias/variance: boosting attacks bias by stacking high-bias,
low-variance stumps. Each stage strictly reduces training loss, which is why it
can overfit and why early stopping is mandatory.

$\lambda$ vs $M$ trade in opposite directions. Halve $\lambda$, roughly
double $M$. Never tune one alone.

Versus random forest: forest = parallel, independent, deep trees,
averaging away variance, hard to overfit, easy to parallelise. Boosting =
sequential, dependent, shallow trees, driving down bias, overfits if unchecked,
usually more accurate on tabular data.
Interview corner
Q. Why is it called gradient boosting when we only fit residuals?

Because the residual is the negative gradient of squared loss with respect to
the prediction. Fitting a tree to it is a gradient-descent step taken in
function space. Swap the loss and the target changes: absolute error gives
$\operatorname{sign}(y-F)$, log loss gives $y-p$. The residual is a special
case, not the definition.
Q. What does the learning rate actually do here?

It shrinks each tree's contribution, so no single tree dominates and the fit
approaches the target through many small corrections. It is a regulariser: the
combination of small $\lambda$ and many trees generalises better than large
$\lambda$ and few trees, at the cost of training time.
Q. Can gradient boosting overfit? How would you tell?

Yes — unlike a random forest. Plot the staged validation score with
staged_predict. Training error keeps falling while validation error
turns upward. Fix with early stopping, lower $\lambda$, shallower trees,
subsample<1, or min_samples_leaf.
Q. Why is the first prediction the mean?

Because the constant that minimises $\sum (y_i - c)^2$ is $c=\bar y$. It is the
best possible zero-feature model, so starting there means every subsequent tree
spends its capacity on structure rather than on the intercept. For log loss the
same argument gives the log-odds.
Q. Why shallow trees?

Boosting needs weak learners. max_depth controls interaction
order: depth 1 gives a purely additive model, depth $d$ allows $d$-way
interactions. Deep trees fit the residuals in one shot, leaving only noise for
later stages, and the ensemble overfits.
Q. Do I need to scale features or encode ordinals carefully?

No scaling — splits are threshold comparisons and are invariant to any
monotone transform. Ordinal encoding is fine for ordered categories; for
unordered high-cardinality categories prefer target/CatBoost encoding or a
library with native categorical support.
